links.comparator_used: Chatbot sessions without human feedback (smokers and vapers had a 20% chance of receiving human feedback between five chatbot sessions)
links.outcome: Retention and effort spent on preparatory activities
links.effect: Having received feedback increased retention and effort on preparatory activities; no numeric effect sizes reported in the abstract. An RL model fit on the data showed some states where not providing feedback was better.
links.tradeoff: Human feedback uses limited human resources, which motivates targeting it. In some states, not providing feedback was better. A benefit-maximizing RL allocation also favours people who are already doing well and want feedback, which raises fairness concerns.
links.quote: We find that having received feedback increases retention and effort spent on preparatory activities.

design_hint: human-in-the-loop support allocation and ethical fairness constraints
